concepts.title: Guerrilla Warfare — Definition and Origins
concepts.excerpt: Guerrilla warfare is the oldest form of organized violence.

concepts.title: Guerrilla Paradox — Why the Weak Win Battles and Lose Wars
concepts.excerpt: Here is the central puzzle of irregular warfare: the strategy that allows a weak force to survive against a stronger one is structurally incompatible with the strategy required to win.

concepts.title: Terrorism vs. Guerrilla Warfare — The Means/Ends Matrix
concepts.excerpt: The words "terrorist" and "guerrilla" are used interchangeably in political speech and often correctly avoided or contested — calling someone a "terrorist" is a political act, not a neutral classification.

concepts.title: Guerrilla Warfare as Historical Norm
concepts.excerpt: Military history as a discipline has a selection bias: it studies the battles that generated decisive outcomes, produced famous commanders, and got written about.

concepts.title: Apolitical/Tribal vs. Ideological/Political Insurgency
concepts.excerpt: A Scottish clansman fighting English occupation in 1297 and a Vietnamese communist fighting French occupation in 1950 are both irregulars, both using guerrilla tactics, both resisting a foreign power.

concepts.title: Insurgent Success Rates — Boot's Database Findings
concepts.excerpt: Boot's most distinctive contribution to the study of insurgency is methodological: he built a database of 443 insurgencies since 1775 and coded each for outcome, duration, ideology type, external support, and other variables.

concepts.title: Counterinsurgency Doctrine — Ancient Origins
concepts.excerpt: The counterinsurgent's dilemma is ancient.

concepts.title: Population-Centric Counterinsurgency Doctrine
concepts.excerpt: The phrase "winning hearts and minds" is often derided as soft-headed idealism — the military equivalent of "can't we all just get along?"

concepts.title: Legitimacy as the Critical Factor in Insurgency and Counterinsurgency
concepts.excerpt: Before asking "who has more firepower?" or "who has better tactics?" or "who has external support?"

concepts.title: Galula and Thompson — The Two Architects of Modern COIN Doctrine
concepts.excerpt: David Galula and Robert Thompson are the two intellectual pillars of modern population-centric counterinsurgency doctrine.

concepts.title: FM 3-24 — The Field Manual That Rediscovered Counterinsurgency
concepts.excerpt: FM 3-24 is the United States Army and Marine Corps field manual on counterinsurgency, published in December 2006 under the direct supervision of General David Petraeus and Lieutenant General James Mattis.

concepts.title: Byzantine Strategikon — The Earliest Surviving Counterinsurgency Manual
concepts.excerpt: The intellectual history of counterinsurgency doctrine usually begins with David Galula's Counterinsurgency Warfare (1964) and Robert Thompson's Defeating Communist Insurgency (1966).

concepts.title: Counterinsurgent Literacy Advantage — Why Documentation Determines Doctrine
concepts.excerpt: Boot's Chapter 12 ("War by the Book") makes an argument that is almost too obvious to notice — and has been almost entirely ignored by military institutional practice.

concepts.title: Rogers's Rangers — The First Written Irregular Warfare Doctrine in American Tradition
concepts.excerpt: Robert Rogers was a New Hampshire frontiersman who, during the French and Indian War (1754–1763), commanded a unit of colonial rangers that operated in ways the British regular army could not.

concepts.title: Outside Support as the Decisive Insurgency Success Factor
concepts.excerpt: If you want to predict whether an insurgency will succeed, Boot's database points to one variable above all others: does it have meaningful outside support?

concepts.title: Conventional Tactics Fail Against Unconventional Threats
concepts.excerpt: A military optimized for conventional warfare has a specific problem when it encounters guerrilla opponents: all its strengths become irrelevancies or liabilities.

concepts.title: Mass Terror — The Limitations of Scorched-Earth Counterinsurgency
concepts.excerpt: The most uncomfortable finding in Boot's analysis is this: mass terror as a counterinsurgency tool has a documented historical success rate.

concepts.title: Public Opinion as the Crucial Insurgent Factor
concepts.excerpt: Before 1776, military victory was usually sufficient to decide political outcomes.

concepts.title: Long Duration — The Timeframe Factor in Insurgencies
concepts.excerpt: One of the most dangerous mistakes a counterinsurgent can make is expecting a quick resolution.

concepts.title: Leadership Decapitation — When Killing the Leader Works
concepts.excerpt: Cult-of-personality dependence: When the movement's coherence depends primarily on the charisma, relationships, and organizational management of a single individual rather than on an ideological program or institutional structure, removing the individual genuinely disrupts the movement.

concepts.title: Technology's Role in Low-Intensity Conflict
concepts.excerpt: Modern counterinsurgency debates frequently center on technology: better surveillance, precision munitions, drone platforms, signals intelligence.

concepts.title: Media War — The Insurgent's Second Battlefield
concepts.excerpt: Every modern insurgency fights two wars simultaneously: the kinetic war against the counterinsurgent's forces and the media war against the counterinsurgent's public.

concepts.title: Chevauchée — Medieval Economic Warfare as Strategic Weapon
concepts.excerpt: The chevauchée (French: "horse charge," but better translated as "mounted raid") was the dominant strategic method of medieval warfare in Western Europe — and it was explicitly guerrilla in its operational logic.

concepts.title: Social Bandits — When Criminality Becomes Proto-Political Insurgency
concepts.excerpt: Not every armed force that opposes a state is an insurgency.

concepts.title: Al-Qaeda — The Franchise Model of Decentralized Insurgency
concepts.excerpt: Al-Qaeda is the most consequential organizational innovation in insurgency history since Mao's people's war doctrine.

concepts.title: Zarqawi's Strategic Failure — Nihilistic Violence Destroys Political Base
concepts.excerpt: Abu Musab al-Zarqawi is Boot's primary case study in insurgent self-destruction.

concepts.title: Scythians vs. Darius — Nomadic Warfare and the Unpunchable Enemy
concepts.excerpt: Around 513 BCE, Darius I of Persia — commanding the largest empire in the ancient world and arguably the most powerful army of the era — led an invasion into the Pontic steppe north of the Black Sea to punish the Scythian nomads who had previously raided Persian territory.

concepts.title: Beth Horon — The Ambush That Started a War (66 CE)
concepts.excerpt: The battle at the pass of Beth Horon in 66 CE is one of the earliest documented cases where a numerically inferior irregular force destroyed a Roman legion through terrain exploitation and ambush — and thereby triggered a decade of catastrophic consequences for both sides.

concepts.title: American Colonial Indian Wars — The School That Shaped the Rangers
concepts.excerpt: The colonial-era conflicts between English settlers and Native American nations (1620s–1760s) were the formative laboratory for American irregular warfare doctrine — the environment in which Rogers's Rangers developed, where the "skulking way of war" was first encountered by European settlers, and where the tension between conventional European military approaches and the tactical demands of North American forest fighting was first experienced with lethal consequences.

concepts.title: The Scottish Jacobite Rebellions — Crushing the Clan System
concepts.excerpt: The Scottish Highland clan system was structurally analogous to the Pashtun tribal system in its key features: loyalty ran vertically to the clan chief rather than horizontally to a national authority; the chief had military obligations from his clansmen and reciprocal obligations of protection; external political authority (the British crown) was accepted when convenient and rejected when it conflicted with clan interest.

concepts.title: The Haitian Revolution — The Insurgency That Shouldn't Have Won
concepts.excerpt: Saint-Domingue (colonial Haiti) was France's most valuable colony in 1791 — producing more sugar and coffee than any comparable territory in the world.

concepts.title: The Peninsular War — Where "Guerrilla" Was Born
concepts.excerpt: "Guerrilla" — the word the English language borrowed to name irregular warfare — means "little war" in Spanish, the diminutive of guerra.

concepts.title: The Greek War of Independence — Nationalism, Great Powers, and the First Modern Insurgency
concepts.excerpt: The Greek revolt of 1821 was organized by the Philike Etairia (Friendly Society) — a secret society of Greek merchants and intellectuals who had been building a nationalist movement for a decade.

concepts.title: Garibaldi — The Guerrilla as National Founding Myth
concepts.excerpt: Giuseppe Garibaldi's expedition of the Thousand (Spedizione dei Mille, 1860) is one of the most audacious military operations in modern history: a force of 1,089 volunteers landing in Sicily and marching through the Kingdom of the Two Sicilies, defeating a regular army of 25,000 within six months, and handing the conquered territory to the Piedmontese king Victor Emmanuel II.

concepts.title: Imam Shamil and the Caucasus — Mountain War, Mountain Faith
concepts.excerpt: Imam Shamil led the Caucasian resistance to Russian imperial expansion from 1834 to 1859 — a sustained guerrilla campaign that occupied Russia's military attention for a generation, tied down hundreds of thousands of troops, and produced the most sophisticated mountain insurgency in 19th-century European history.

concepts.title: The First Afghan War — The Graveyard of Empires' First Burial
concepts.excerpt: In January 1842, a British Indian Army column of approximately 16,500 soldiers, camp followers, and dependents began retreating from Kabul toward Jalalabad through the Khyber Pass in winter.

concepts.title: The Pashtun Northwest Frontier — A Century of Unwinnable War
concepts.excerpt: The British Northwest Frontier (roughly modern Pakistan's tribal belt and eastern Afghanistan) was the most continuous military problem in British imperial history — a century-long series of expeditions, punitive operations, garrisons, political agreements, and renewed insurgencies that consumed enormous resources without producing lasting pacification.

concepts.title: Lyautey in Morocco — The COIN Commander Who Built a Country
concepts.excerpt: Hubert Lyautey is Boot's most admired historical COIN practitioner — the French general who developed a population-centric approach to colonial pacification in Madagascar and Morocco decades before Galula formalized the theory.

concepts.title: The Boer War — When the Empire Met the Commando
concepts.excerpt: The Second Boer War (1899–1902) is the case that forced the British Empire to confront the gap between its conventional military dominance and its capacity to fight an irregular war.

concepts.title: T.E. Lawrence and the Arab Revolt — The Theory of the Sideshow
concepts.excerpt: T. E.

concepts.title: Orde Wingate — The Eccentric Who Invented Special Forces
concepts.excerpt: Orde Wingate was one of the most tactically innovative and institutionally disruptive military officers of the 20th century — a man whose ideas were decades ahead of doctrine, whose methods generated results that conventional military thinking couldn't explain, and who died in a plane crash in Burma in 1944 before he could consolidate the institutional legacy his innovations deserved.

concepts.title: Tito's Partisans — Resistance in the Most Hostile Environment
concepts.excerpt: Josip Broz Tito led the Yugoslav Partisans from 1941 to the liberation of Yugoslavia in 1945 — conducting one of the most successful resistance campaigns in occupied Europe against German, Italian, and Ustasha forces that collectively outnumbered his forces many times over.

concepts.title: Mao and the Chinese Revolution — People's War as Political System
concepts.excerpt: Mao Zedong's most quoted maxim on guerrilla warfare — "The guerrilla must move among the people as a fish swims in the sea" — is simultaneously a military metaphor and a political program.

concepts.title: Dien Bien Phu — When the Guerrilla Stopped Being One
concepts.excerpt: On May 7, 1954, French forces at Dien Bien Phu surrendered to Viet Minh forces under General Vo Nguyen Giap — ending 56 days of siege, the immediate French military presence in Indochina, and the First Indochina War.

concepts.title: Malaya — The COIN Campaign That Actually Worked
concepts.excerpt: The Malayan Emergency (1948–1960) is Boot's primary positive case study for population-centric counterinsurgency — the closest thing to a textbook success in the modern COIN literature.

concepts.title: Algeria — How to Win Every Battle and Lose the War
concepts.excerpt: The French military campaign in Algeria (1954–1962) is Boot's clearest case of tactical COIN success producing strategic defeat.

concepts.title: Edward Lansdale in the Philippines — COIN as Governance
concepts.excerpt: Edward Lansdale is Boot's model COIN practitioner — the rare American military officer who understood, in the late 1940s and early 1950s, what the counterinsurgency problem actually was and who implemented a comprehensive response that worked.

concepts.title: Lansdale in Vietnam — The COIN Advisor Without a Partner
concepts.excerpt: Edward Lansdale's Vietnam assignment (1954–1956, then 1965–1968) is Boot's case study in the limits of advisory COIN — the moment when the best-available American practitioner of population-centric counterinsurgency discovered that doctrine without a compatible political partner is inert.

concepts.title: The Cuban Revolution — The Insurgency That Made Theory
concepts.excerpt: Corrupt at every level: Military officers were political appointees whose primary activity was personal enrichment.

concepts.title: Che Guevara and Foco Theory — The Model That Killed Its Author
concepts.excerpt: Ernesto "Che" Guevara's Guerrilla Warfare (1960) and Régis Debray's Revolution in the Revolution?

concepts.title: Vietnam — The War Firepower Couldn't Win
concepts.excerpt: The United States dropped more bombs on Indochina between 1965 and 1975 than were dropped by all sides in World War II combined.

concepts.title: Petraeus and the Iraq Surge — COIN Applied Under Pressure
concepts.excerpt: The 2007–2008 Iraq Surge is Boot's most recent and most thoroughly documented COIN case study — the moment when the US military applied FM 3-24's population-centric framework at scale under wartime conditions and achieved measurable results.

concepts.title: Shadow Governance Infrastructure
concepts.excerpt: Here is the plain version: most movements, when they win power, arrive at the levers of government and discover they have no idea how to pull them.
